About

I finished my M.S. in Mechanical Engineering at NYU Tandon in May 2026 with a 3.73 GPA. Before that I read Mechanical Engineering at MJCET in Hyderabad, where I captained the SAE team and founded a technical society that grew from nothing to more than a hundred members.

The through-line in my work is the handoff between a design that exists on a screen and a thing that can actually be built. At Advance Tooling Systems I evaluated draft, wall thickness and tooling feasibility across fifty-plus units and found that recurring fitment defects were coming from gaps in dimensional inspection rather than from the tools themselves; revising those checkpoints cut rework by 10 to 15 per cent. At Mahindra I mapped a multi-stage assembly line station by station. At Ingentas Robotics, a company I co-founded, I packaged motors, controllers, sensor modules and wire harnesses into machined and 3D-printed enclosures and delivered all eight builds on time.

I am also comfortable being wrong in public. My undergraduate capstone failed on ten-inch stairs and the whole team, me included, assumed the motors were undersized. The statics showed a 2.4× torque margin at the failure point. The real limit was traction. That habit, checking the explanation everyone agrees on, has been more useful to me than most of what I have built.

On the analysis side I work in SolidWorks Flow Simulation and ANSYS, but the part I care about is the check afterwards. Outside coursework I took five applied fluid and heat transfer problems and hand-calculated every one from theory before I accepted what the solver returned. The counter-current heat exchanger matched the LMTD calculation to 0.007 per cent and the venturi came within 1.16 per cent of ISO 5167-4. Nobody assigned that work. I wanted to know whether I could trust my own numbers before anyone else had to.

Most of what I know about building things I learned by building them badly first. I assembled an FDM 3D printer from bare stepper motors, drivers, a heated bed and frame hardware, squared the axes, configured the firmware and debugged it until it printed reliably. I have modelled a 30-part motorcycle from scratch and drawn all thirty manufacturing drawings myself. None of that was coursework either.

I have also run teams. I captained a fifteen-plus member SAE team to second place nationally at IPEC 2K23 across three national competitions, and founded a technical society that went from zero to more than a hundred members and twenty-five events on two thousand dollars of sponsorship. Both taught me the same thing: a schedule is a design constraint, and the person holding it has to be the one who understands the parts.

I am looking for full-time work in manufacturing, process and product development engineering, ideally somewhere the design desk is close enough to the shop floor that I can walk over and look at the thing. If that sounds like your team, the contact details are at the bottom of this page.

Selected work

SHEET01

Full motorcycle design and assembly

SolidWorks · Jul – Aug 2026 · Independent project

A complete motorcycle modelled part by part over three weeks: 30 unique components, three subassemblies and one top-level assembly. The build exercised the parts of SolidWorks that production work actually depends on: weldment structural members for the frame, surfacing for the fuel tank as a 2 mm thin-wall body, and cast-part detailing on the crank case cover with a 74° draft and a four-bolt circle on a 102 mm square pattern.

I then produced all 30 manufacturing drawings myself from my own models, with section and detail views, specifying tube geometry, draft angles, bolt patterns and stepped bore dimensions.

SHEET02

Stair-climbing robot: belt drive design and failure analysis

B.E. capstone · 2024 · Team of three

A tracked, belt-driven platform on a 6061-T6 aluminium frame: four belt drives, eight Ø60 mm pulleys with 10 mm grooves, four 300 rpm geared DC motors, Arduino Uno and HC-05 control. The belt system went through two profile iterations before the toothed profile was adopted.

We tested it past its working limit rather than stopping at the last success, recording speed and power draw at each stair rise.

Test matrix, tread fixed at 10 in
Stair riseSpeedPowerResult
4 in0.25 m/s60 WStable
6 in0.20 m/s70 WStable
8 in0.15 m/s85 WPartially stable, slipping
10 inn/an/aFailed to climb

The team's first reading was insufficient motor torque. The statics disagreed: required torque falls as the incline steepens, because normal force scales with cos θ. At the 45.5° failure point the drivetrain needed about 2.06 N·m and the motors supplied 5 N·m, roughly a 2.4× margin. The limiting factor was traction and stability, not power, so the remaining work went into track compliance and centre of mass instead of a drivetrain redesign.

2.4× torque margin at failure4-point test matrixRoot cause corrected
SHEET03

Applied CFD and heat transfer portfolio

SolidWorks Flow Simulation · 2026 · Self-directed

Five applied fluid and heat transfer problems solved in Flow Simulation and hand-calculated from theory first, so the solver was checked against the analysis rather than trusted on its own: a reduction nozzle, loss coefficient across a ball valve, a counter-current heat exchanger, indoor air change under ventilation load, and a venturi flowmeter.

The ball valve study swept inlet velocity from 0.1 to 10 m/s at four opening angles and reduced each run to a loss coefficient. Plotted against Reynolds number the curves flatten above roughly Re 30,000, which is the behaviour the textbook predicts and a useful check that the model was set up correctly.

Heat exchanger within 0.007% of LMTDVenturi within 1.16% of ISO 5167-4
CFDHeat transferPressure dropPsychrometricsAnalytical validation
SHEET04

TerraExplorer: six-wheel remote sensing rover

MJCET R&D Cell · Oct 2023 – May 2024 · Four-person team

I was the only mechanical engineer on an otherwise all-electronics team. I designed the chassis and rocker-bogie suspension in SolidWorks around 20 × 20 mm aluminium T-slot profile, 20 mm aluminium tube and 3D-printed joints, then printed and assembled the running vehicle. Steering used an Ackermann layout; the rover is remote-operated over RF with an FPV video feed.

The project was funded by the MJCET R&D Department and received the R&D Cell's Letter of Appreciation.

Rocker-bogie suspensionAckermann steeringT-slot chassisFDM printed jointsArduino MEGA
SHEET05

Solar desalination plant: CSP with multi-effect distillation

Thermal system design and financial model · 2024

A 500,000 litre-per-day desalination plant driven by a concentrated solar power tower with eight hours of molten salt thermal storage. I ran the thermal calculations across the solar field, the storage block and the MED train, then built the supporting case: $27M CAPEX, a 10 to 12 year break-even and a 30-year design life, sizing the plant against both thermal performance and project economics.

500,000 L/day$27M CAPEX8 h molten salt storage

SHEET07

Kinematic gear drive vehicle

NYU Tandon · fully 3D-printed assembly · Grade A

A 20-part fully printed vehicle built around a three-stage gear train. I ran a worst-case tolerance stack-up across the train and specified ±0.15 mm running clearances to absorb FDM dimensional variation and guarantee backlash-free meshing, then iterated three print cycles to a fully operational prototype.
